design_detail: Opportunistic longitudinal follow-up of people first tested in two earlier studies from the same unit (Curran & Morgan, 2000; Curran & Monaghan, 2001), which the authors call an independent group longitudinal design (p. 1452). Baseline is the drug-free session those studies held 3 days after a night on which the ketamine participants had taken ketamine; the follow-up, 3–4 years later, repeats the same battery with alternate test versions. Analysed: 18 people from the original ketamine groups, all of whom had cut their use, and 10 polydrug controls. Group (ketamine, control) × time (baseline, follow-up) repeated-measures ANOVAs, Mann–Whitney tests and correlations of change scores (pp. 1452–1454). There is no group that continued using ketamine.
can_establish: In this small re-contacted sample, whether group differences present 3 days after ketamine use were still present 3–4 years later, after a self-reported fall in frequency of use, relative to polydrug controls retested on the same tasks over the same interval.
cannot_establish: That ketamine caused the baseline or the persisting differences (there is no measurement before use, and the persisting differences were present at baseline and did not change, which fits pre-existing differences as well as lasting effects, as the authors concede for episodic memory, p. 1458); that cutting down caused the improvement in category fluency (no group continued using, and the baseline, taken 3 days after use, may include after-effects of that use); or anything about the 38 original ketamine participants who could not be contacted (p. 1459).

sample.recruitment: Originally recruited at nightclubs and parties by snowball sampling for the two earlier studies. 33 of the 76 original participants could be contacted and all but 2 agreed, 19 of them from the original ketamine groups (p. 1452).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Participation in one of the two earlier studies. Excluded: one member of the original ketamine group who had since developed schizophrenia, and two polydrug controls who had started using ketamine (p. 1452). No other criteria are stated. No abstinence requirement before the follow-up session and no ethics committee approval are reported; participants gave written, witnessed informed consent (p. 1452).
sample.demographics: Ketamine group: 18 (4 women); mean age 28.1; spot-the-word score 48.38 (SD 3.46). Controls: 10 (6 women); mean age 26.5; spot-the-word 50.12 (3.16). The dispersions printed for age (0.81 and 0.70) are too small to be standard deviations (see reporting issues). HADS anxiety 7.89 (4.96) vs 6.63 (3.74); HADS depression 5.27 (4.32) vs 2.00 (2.45) (Table 1 and Results › Demographics, p. 1454). Education and occupation are not reported for this sample.
sample.attrition: 33 of the 76 original participants could be contacted (p. 1452), and 38 members of the original ketamine group could not be (p. 1459). The two earlier papers report 20 + 37 ketamine participants and 19 controls (Curran & Morgan, 2000, p. 577; Curran & Monaghan, 2001, p. 751), so 18 of 57 (32%) of the ketamine participants and 10 of 19 (53%) of the controls were analysed, which also implies that the 2 who declined were controls (editors' calculation). Completers are not compared with those lost on their baseline scores.
sample.selection_effects: Strongly selected. About a third of the original ketamine participants were analysed, all of whom had reduced their use; the authors note that many could not be contacted because of transient lifestyles and that those lost may have continued using (p. 1459). The one participant with the most severe outcome (schizophrenia) was excluded, and so were the two controls who had started using ketamine. The ketamine group combines participants from both earlier studies, one of which compared frequent with infrequent use, in proportions that are not reported; all controls came from Curran & Morgan (2000), whose controls had little or no prior ketamine use (p. 577 of that paper). The sex ratio differs (22% vs 60% women; Fisher's exact P = 0.10, editors' calculation) and is not adjusted for.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at follow-up: current drug use and questions on patterns of ketamine use such as craving and periods of abstinence (p. 1452); the baseline frequency comes from the original studies. No hair or urine analysis at follow-up; the authors state that retrospective estimates are inevitably inaccurate and could not be checked objectively (p. 1459).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported. Frequency of ketamine use fell from a mean of 6.45 (SD 8.13) days per month at baseline to 1.61 (3.19) at follow-up, reported as an average reduction of 88.3%; 8 of 18 had not used ketamine for more than 6 months; the reported amount per occasion rose from 0.31 (0.25) g at baseline to 0.44 (0.97) g at follow-up (Results › Drug use, p. 1454). Duration of use, route and purity are not reported. None had escalated or kept the same level of use (p. 1459).
exposure.polysubstance: Both groups used other drugs (Table 2, p. 1454): regular cannabis use 77.8% vs 80%, alcohol 94.4% vs 100%, MDMA 72.2% vs 60%, cocaine 61.1% vs 50%, with no significant differences in these proportions or in days per month of use; amounts were not analysed because the estimates could not be standardized; there was a trend for longer cannabis use in the ketamine group (U = 46.5, P = 0.052). Other current use: amphetamines (4 in the ketamine group, 1 control), benzodiazepines (1 and 1), LSD or psilocybin (2 and 1) (p. 1454). No other drug was adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported for the follow-up session: no required interval since last use and no urine screen are described, and 10 of the 18 in the ketamine group had used ketamine within the previous 6 months (p. 1454). The baseline session was held 3 days after a night of drug use (p. 1452).

comparison.controls: 10 polydrug controls from the control group of Curran & Morgan (2000), recruited in the same party and club settings and retested on the same schedule (p. 1452).
comparison.matching: Not matched by design. The authors describe the groups as well matched on drug use, IQ and age (p. 1457) and on other drug use and demographic variables (p. 1459). The sex ratio differs, education is not reported for this sample, and HADS depression was higher in the ketamine group at follow-up.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measurement before ketamine use: the baseline itself followed recent use in people with a history of use. Premorbid ability only as a current reading-based estimate (spot-the-word). Family psychiatric history and childhood adversity are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls used cannabis, alcohol, MDMA and cocaine at rates similar to the ketamine group (Table 2, p. 1454); their lifetime ketamine use is not reported in this paper.

outcomes.instruments: All measured in drug-free sessions; nothing was measured during intoxication. Semantic memory: speed of comprehension (sentences marked as sensible or not within 2 minutes; number judged correctly and errors; described here as 200 sentences, see reporting issues) and category fluency (members of a category named in 90 seconds; correct exemplars, perseverative and semantic errors). Episodic memory: prose recall from the Rivermead Behavioural Memory Test, immediately and after a filled delay of about 20 minutes (idea units, maximum 21). Executive and attentional tasks: digit cancellation (time to cross out every 4 among 400 digits; omission and commission errors), serial sevens (subtractions in 90 seconds; errors) and letter fluency (words in 90 seconds; perseverative and alphabetical errors). Self-ratings: the Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire (state schizotypal symptoms); a dissociative states scale (introduced as the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale, analysed as an adapted scale total); Bond–Lader mood visual analogue scales (three factors); a 14-item visual analogue scale of bodily, perceptual and cognitive symptoms associated with ketamine; the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale for the past week. Spot-the-word as an estimate of premorbid verbal IQ (pp. 1452–1453).
outcomes.validity_norms: Published tests (Rivermead prose recall, speed of comprehension, HADS, spot-the-word) alongside two of the authors' own state scales (the schizotypal questionnaire and the subjective-effects scale, from Curran & Morgan, 2000), which have no norms. Scores are compared only with the 10 controls, never with norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment or deficit means a lower score than the 10 polydrug controls (a main effect of group across both sessions); recovery means a group × time interaction with no group difference at follow-up; persisting means a main effect of group without an interaction. No clinical threshold is applied.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. About 23 scores were tested at P < 0.05 (13 cognitive scores and 10 self-rating scores); correlations were limited to measures with significant group effects or interactions, which the authors present as a guard against Type 1 errors (p. 1454).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The first author interviewed participants (epigraph, p. 1451), and group membership was known from the earlier studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Test statistics without confidence intervals; means for the main measures (category fluency, sentences judged, prose recall) appear only as bars with standard errors (Figures 1–3). Category fluency: group × time F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032; baseline difference t = 2.42, P = 0.023; no difference at follow-up (p. 1454). Speed of comprehension: group F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007; errors group × time F(1,26) = 4.35, P = 0.047 (p. 1455). Prose recall: group F(1,26) = 4.36, P = 0.047 (immediate) and 4.43, P = 0.045 (delayed) (p. 1456). Digit cancellation: group F(1,26) = 7.09, P = 0.013; ketamine group 66.01 (14.12) and 65.32 (11.34) s against controls 54.60 (7.82) and 55.97 (8.74) s (p. 1456). Schizotypal symptoms: group F(1,26) = 15.32, P = 0.001; time F(1,26) = 59.25, P < 0.001 (p. 1456). Subjective-effects factors at follow-up: U = 34, 21 and 39.5 (P = 0.007, 0.001 and 0.014) (p. 1456). Change in category fluency correlated with change in ketamine use (r = 0.712) and with time since last use (r = 0.723), both P < 0.002 (p. 1457). Editors' calculation (pooled SD; 95% CI by the large-sample approximation): digit cancellation d ≈ 0.93 (0.12 to 1.74) at baseline and 0.89 (0.08 to 1.70) at follow-up; schizotypal score d ≈ 1.49 at baseline and 1.05 (0.23 to 1.87) at follow-up; HADS depression d ≈ 0.87 (0.06 to 1.67); for r = 0.712 with n = 18 (Fisher z), 95% CI 0.37 to 0.88.
analysis.covariates: None, apart from a re-analysis of digit cancellation time adjusting for errors, which did not change the result (p. 1456).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: No group × time test is reported for prose recall or for the number of sentences judged correctly, although the abstract describes improved semantic memory and persisting episodic deficits; the improvement in sentences judged rests on inspection of Figure 2 (p. 1455). Means and standard deviations for these measures are not printed. Correlations with cannabis and alcohol use were planned (p. 1454) but are not reported, and the number of correlations run is not stated. The four dissociation factors named in the Method are not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 18 and 10 participants only large differences can be detected; the absence of differences on dissociation, mood, serial sevens and letter fluency is uninformative.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 28 of the 76 original participants, the ketamine group's lower category fluency 3 days after use was no longer different from the controls' 3–4 years later, after a self-reported fall in frequency of use, and the gain in category fluency correlated with the reduction in use and with time since last use. Prose recall, digit cancellation time and the number of sentences judged were lower in the ketamine group across both sessions, without a reported change over time; the controls' delayed recall fell at follow-up, leaving a gap of under one idea unit (editors' reading of Figure 3). State schizotypy was higher in the ketamine group at both sessions and fell in both groups. At follow-up the ketamine group rated more perceptual, bodily and cognitive symptoms and more depressive symptoms than the controls.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that semantic memory impairments are reversible on marked reduction of use, that episodic and possibly attentional impairments appear long-lasting, that schizotypal symptoms and perceptual distortions may persist after cessation, and that people who use or might use ketamine should be aware of its “enduring effects” on memory and experience (p. 1450). The Discussion attributes the baseline semantic differences to ketamine because the groups were matched on drug use, IQ and age (p. 1457), yet concedes that the persisting episodic deficit could be pre-existing (p. 1458) and that it is unclear whether the schizotypal elevation is pre-existing or a chronic effect (p. 1459). Differences present at the drug-free baseline that did not change cannot separate a lasting drug effect from a pre-existing difference, and since 10 of the 18 had used ketamine within the previous 6 months the data cannot show persistence after cessation. The attentional claim rests on slower digit cancellation without more errors, which the authors themselves say may be general slowing (p. 1458). The semantic recovery rests on one interaction in 28 people, with no group that continued using and a baseline taken 3 days after use, and the improvement in sentences judged is read from a figure. The inference of a “low potential for dependence” (p. 1459) is drawn from people who were selected by having cut down and could still be contacted.

timeline.event: Baseline source for 20 of the original ketamine participants and all controls: 3 days after use, the ketamine group scored lower than polydrug controls on semantic memory tasks and higher on dissociation and schizotypy

Baseline source for the other 37 original ketamine participants (18 frequent, 19 infrequent; no control group): 3 days after use, the frequent group was more impaired than the infrequent group on episodic and semantic memory tasks

Cross-sectional study of 150 people from the same unit: no group differences in prose recall or category fluency, including the ex-ketamine group; the authors suggest the prose recall deficits of the earlier day-0 and day-3 designs may have reflected a lack of practice effects (pp. 82–85)
One-year follow-up of the 2009 sample: no group differences in prose recall, and no cognitive deficits in the abstinent group at either session

replication.where_it_stands: This follow-up remains a single, small and highly selected sample, and no independent longitudinal replication appears among the sources read for this card (later studies were not searched by this reader). In the same unit's larger studies, prose recall and category fluency did not differ between people with frequent, infrequent or past ketamine use and controls (Morgan et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2010b), so the persisting episodic memory deficit reported here is not supported by the same group's later data. The absence of deficits in the 2009 ex-ketamine group is consistent with, but does not test, the recovery of category fluency reported here.

funding.funder: Medical Research Council (UK) studentship to C.J.A.M. (Acknowledgements, p. 1460).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors were at the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London, which ran both baseline studies; the second author was second author of one of them (Curran & Monaghan, 2001).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that tests people before they start using ketamine and at intervals afterwards, with a comparison group matched on other drug use and tested at the same intervals, ketamine use and abstinence verified by hair and urine analysis, enough people who continue, reduce and stop to compare them, assessors blind to group, and means reported for every measure.

domains.note: No adjustment for any variable. The sex ratio differs, education is not reported, HADS depression differs at follow-up and ability before use is unknown; the claimed matching on age and other drug use cannot be checked, because the printed dispersions appear to be standard errors.

Ketamine use and its change over 3–4 years rest entirely on self-report, retrospective at both sessions, with no biological verification; the authors call such estimates inevitably inaccurate (p. 1459). The method behind the reported 88.3% reduction is not stated.

Only 33 of 76 could be contacted, and 18 of 57 original ketamine participants were analysed (editors' calculation), all of whom had cut down; those lost may have kept using (p. 1459), and the participant who developed schizophrenia was excluded. Selection is related to the exposure (change in use) and plausibly to the outcomes.

Whether anyone received treatment for drug use between the sessions, and what else changed in their lives, is not reported; the authors attribute the fall in schizotypy and dissociation in both groups to age and lifestyle (p. 1459).
About two thirds of the original participants are missing at follow-up, with no comparison of their baseline scores against those of completers.

Standard tasks with alternate versions, but testers were not blind to group, two self-rating scales are the authors' own, and some error scores were at floor; the descriptions of two tasks differ from the baseline study's (see reporting issues).

Means not printed for the main outcomes; interaction tests not reported for prose recall and sentences judged; planned correlations with cannabis and alcohol use not reported; dissociation factors not reported; several table cells appear duplicated or contradict the text.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design cannot answer its own question: with no group that continued using, and with about a third of the original ketamine participants retained, selected by having cut down, neither recovery nor persistence can be attributed to the change in ketamine use. The persisting differences were already present at the drug-free baseline and did not change, which fits pre-existing differences as well as lasting drug effects, and practice, regression toward the mean and after-effects at the 3-day baseline are uncontrolled. The source may be cited as a description of what this follow-up observed (category fluency no longer different after reduced use; lower prose recall and slower digit cancellation at both sessions; higher state schizotypy and subjective symptoms), with its limits stated; it should not be cited for reversibility, for lasting effects of ketamine, or for a low potential for dependence.

key_findings.finding: Of the 76 participants of the two earlier studies, 33 could be contacted and all but 2 agreed, 19 of them from the original ketamine groups; after excluding one person who had developed schizophrenia and two controls who had started using ketamine, 18 from the ketamine groups and 10 polydrug controls were retested 3–4 years after their first testing.
key_findings.note: The Discussion adds that 38 members of the original ketamine group could not be contacted (p. 1459, Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph). With 57 original ketamine participants and 19 controls in the two earlier papers, 18 of 57 (32%) and 10 of 19 (53%) were analysed (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The ketamine group reported using ketamine on 1.61 (SD 3.19) days per month at follow-up against 6.45 (SD 8.13) at baseline, described as an average reduction in frequency of 88.3%; 8 of 18 had not used ketamine for more than 6 months, and the reported amount per occasion had risen from 0.31 (0.25) g to 0.44 (0.97) g.
key_findings.note: Self-report only. The group means imply a 75% fall in mean frequency; the method behind 88.3% (perhaps the mean of individual reductions) is not stated (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Category fluency showed a group × time interaction (F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032) and a main effect of time (F(1,26) = 7.50, P = 0.011): the ketamine group generated fewer category members than controls at baseline (t = 2.42, P = 0.023) but not at follow-up. Perseverative errors were more frequent in the ketamine group at both sessions (group F(1,26) = 6.13, P = 0.02): 1.94 (2.36) vs 0.5 (0.71) at baseline and 1.29 (2.29) vs 0.4 (0.68) at follow-up; semantic errors were at floor at follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks › Semantic memory, 1st paragraph (p. 1454, continuing on p. 1455); Table 3 and Figure 1 (p. 1455)
key_findings.note: Group means appear only as bars with standard errors (Figure 1). Editors' reading of Figure 1 at 300 dpi: about 16 vs 21 category members at baseline and about 20 vs 21 at follow-up. The t statistic is printed with df 1,27 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: On speed of comprehension the ketamine group judged fewer sentences correctly than controls across both sessions (group F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007); no interaction is reported for this score, and the authors describe an apparent increase in the ketamine group from Figure 2. Errors showed a group × time interaction (F(1,26) = 4.35, P = 0.047): more errors in the ketamine group at baseline (1.06 (1.12) vs 0.2 (0.42)) but not at follow-up (0.38 (0.46) vs 0.4 (0.52)), when errors were at floor.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks › Speed of comprehension task, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 2 at 300 dpi: about 62 vs 86 sentences judged correctly at baseline and about 73 vs 83 at follow-up.

key_findings.finding: Prose recall showed a main effect of group (immediate F(1,26) = 4.36, P = 0.047; delayed F(1,26) = 4.43, P = 0.045), the ketamine group recalling less across both sessions; no group × time result is reported, and the authors note that the controls' delayed recall fell at follow-up (Figure 3b).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks › Episodic memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: Means appear only as bars on axes that start at 4 idea units. Editors' reading of Figure 3 at 300 dpi: immediate recall about 7.9 vs 10.3 idea units at baseline and 7.4 vs 8.9 at follow-up; delayed recall about 7.2 vs 9.7 and 7.4 vs 8.2. The follow-up gap in delayed recall is under one idea unit (maximum score 21), so the main effect rests largely on the baseline difference; no test of the follow-up difference is reported.

key_findings.finding: Digit cancellation was slower in the ketamine group at both sessions (group F(1,26) = 7.09, P = 0.013; no interaction or effect of time): 66.01 (14.12) s at baseline and 65.32 (11.34) s at follow-up, against 54.60 (7.82) and 55.97 (8.74) s in controls; errors did not differ, and adjusting for errors did not change the result (editors' calculation: d ≈ 0.93 at baseline and 0.89 at follow-up).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks › Digit cancellation, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors say the slower time may reflect general psychomotor slowing rather than an attentional impairment (p. 1458, Discussion › Attention and working memory, 1st paragraph). The ketamine group mixes participants of the two earlier studies in proportions that are not reported, and the authors note that those from Curran & Monaghan (2001) already had poorer attentional functioning at the first session than those from Curran & Morgan (2000), whose ketamine group had shown no attentional difference from its controls 3 days after use (p. 1458); the 10 controls came from the original polydrug control group (p. 1452). The slower times at both sessions may therefore partly reflect who came from which study.

key_findings.finding: There were no group differences at either session on letter fluency (baseline 19.8 (6.23) vs 21 (5.94) words; follow-up 21 (5.62) vs 20.4 (4.01)) or serial sevens (baseline 24.8 (8.16) vs 20.78 (10.17) subtractions; follow-up 22 (9.33) vs 23 (7.97)); perseverative errors in letter fluency showed a trend towards more in the ketamine group (F(1,26) = 3.30, P = 0.081).
key_findings.locator: Results › Executive functioning › Serial sevens and verbal fluency, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The ketamine group's baseline serial sevens value, 24.8 (8.16), is identical to the controls' baseline schizotypal total in Table 4 (p. 1455); one of the two may be a transcription error.

key_findings.finding: State schizotypal symptoms (Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire) were higher in the ketamine group than in controls across both sessions (group F(1,26) = 15.32, P = 0.001) and fell in both groups (time F(1,26) = 59.25, P < 0.001), without an interaction: totals 51.5 (21.28) vs 24.8 (8.16) at baseline and 18.67 (17.05) vs 4.0 (4.06) at follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective measures (Table 4) › Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire, 1st paragraph (p. 1456); Table 4 (p. 1455)
key_findings.note: The scale indexes state rather than trait schizotypy, and schizotypal scores did not correlate with ketamine use (p. 1459, Discussion › Subjective effects, 1st paragraph). Editors' calculation: d ≈ 1.49 at baseline and 1.05 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.87) at follow-up.

key_findings.finding: Dissociative-states scores fell in both groups (time F(1,26) = 5.93, P = 0.022) with no group difference (totals 10.11 (15.38) vs 5.44 (5.85) at baseline and 3.24 (4.53) vs 0.80 (1.54) at follow-up); the text reports no group differences on any of the three mood factors at either session.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective measures › Adapted Dissociative States Scale and Mood Rating Scale paragraphs (p. 1456); Table 4 (p. 1455)
key_findings.note: The dissociation measure is introduced in the Method as the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale (p. 1453) but analysed as an adapted scale total, and Table 4 marks baseline mood differences that the text denies (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: At follow-up the ketamine group rated more perceptual (U = 34, P = 0.007), bodily (U = 21, P = 0.001) and cognitive or mental-state symptoms (U = 39.5, P = 0.014) than controls on the 14-item visual analogue subjective-effects scale: perceptual 8.4 (7.71) vs 1.18 (1.45), somatic 9.33 (7.14) vs 1.14 (1.25), cognitive 14.47 (14.89) vs 3.75 (3.95).
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective measures › Subjective Effects Scale, 1st paragraph (p. 1456); Table 4 (p. 1455)
key_findings.note: The perceptual difference was at least as large at baseline (13.43 (9.20) vs 1.12 (1.56); editors' calculation, Welch t ≈ 5.5), although Table 4 marks no baseline significance; the follow-up difference therefore does not show a change over time, and 10 of the 18 had used ketamine in the previous 6 months.

key_findings.finding: At follow-up the ketamine group scored higher than controls on HADS depression (5.27 (4.32) vs 2.00 (2.45); U = 55.5, P < 0.031) but not on HADS anxiety (7.89 (4.96) vs 6.63 (3.74)); change in depression cannot be assessed because one of the two earlier studies did not use the HADS.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics (Table 1), 1st paragraph, and Table 1 (p. 1454); Discussion › Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph (p. 1459)
key_findings.note: The authors state that the ketamine group was not within a clinical range of depression (p. 1459) but give no cut-off or individual scores. Editors' calculation: d ≈ 0.87 (95% CI 0.06 to 1.67). The printed test does not reproduce: U = 55.5 with 18 and 10 participants gives a two-tailed p of about 0.10 (reporting issue 8).

key_findings.finding: Change in category fluency (follow-up minus baseline) correlated with change in ketamine use (r = 0.712, P < 0.002) and with time since last ketamine use (r = 0.723, P < 0.002); the sample used and the sign convention for change in use are not stated. Digit cancellation did not correlate with immediate or delayed recall.
key_findings.note: The Method says correlations were also run within the ketamine group (p. 1454). Editors' calculation for n = 18: 95% CI 0.37 to 0.88 for r = 0.712. Those who used most at baseline had the most room both to cut down and to improve, so regression toward the mean is not excluded.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the persisting episodic memory deficit could be due either to pre-existing differences or to ketamine use (p. 1458), that it is unclear whether the higher schizotypal scores reflect pre-existing differences or chronic effects of ketamine (p. 1459), and that pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out without prospective studies (p. 1459).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Episodic memory, 1st paragraph (p. 1458); Discussion › Subjective effects, 1st paragraph, and Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph (p. 1459)

key_findings.finding: None of the 18 had escalated or kept the same level of ketamine use, and all reported few problems in cutting down, which the authors read as a low potential for dependence; they acknowledge that the 38 uncontacted members of the original ketamine group may have continued using and that a group continuing ketamine use would have been the right comparison.
One member of the original ketamine group had developed schizophrenia by the time of follow-up and was excluded (p. 1452); the Discussion presents this case as anecdotal evidence (p. 1459).
key_findings.locator: Method, 1st paragraph (p. 1452); Discussion › Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (p. 1459)
key_findings.note: The Discussion places this person within the sample of 18, although the Method excluded them before the 18 were counted (see reporting issues). A single excluded case gives no estimate of risk.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 is headed as giving standard deviations, but its age dispersions (0.81 and 0.70 years, for means of 28.1 and 26.5) are too small to be standard deviations if, as the text says, the groups did not differ in age; the text also reports no group differences in days per month of alcohol use (16.67 (2.69) vs 13.70 (3.23)) or cocaine use (2.28 (0.94) vs 1.00 (0.44)) in Table 2. Editors' calculation: read as SDs, these give Welch t ≈ 5.5 (P < 0.001) for age, 2.5 (P ≈ 0.03) for alcohol and 4.9 (P < 0.001) for cocaine; read as standard errors, the age difference gives t ≈ 1.5 (P ≈ 0.15). Other rows, such as years since first cannabis use (9.94 (5.94)), behave like SDs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot tell which dispersions are standard deviations and which standard errors, so the matching on age and other drug use on which the authors rest their attribution to ketamine cannot be checked; if the printed values are SDs, the groups were not matched on age, alcohol or cocaine use.

reporting_issues.issue: The baseline category fluency comparison is printed as t(1,27) = 2.42; an independent t-test with 18 and 10 participants has 26 degrees of freedom (the printed P = 0.023 fits either).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the F tests correctly use df 1,26.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline reduction in frequency of ketamine use (88.3%, in the abstract and Results) does not follow from the printed group means of 6.45 and 1.61 days per month, and the method of calculation is not stated (editors' calculation: the means imply a 75% fall).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 88.3% figure should be cited, if at all, as the authors' average of a reduction computed in an unstated way; individual changes in use are not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The dissociation measure is introduced as the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale with four factors (p. 1453) but reported as an adapted scale total, labelled ADSS in Table 4 and ADDS in the text (pp. 1455–1456); one of the baseline studies describes the adapted version as the 19 self-rated items of that scale (Curran & Monaghan, 2001, p. 752). The three mood factors are named alertness, calmness and discontentedness in the Method (p. 1453), sedation, discontentedness and calm in Table 4, and drowsiness, discontentedness and anxiety in the Results (p. 1456).
reporting_issues.consequence: The dissociation results come from a self-rated adaptation, not from the clinician-administered scale, and should not be cited as CADSS scores; the mood factors cannot be identified with certainty.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports no group differences on any mood factor at either session (p. 1456), but Table 4 marks baseline differences in discontentedness (21.47 vs 37.92, P < 0.01) and calm (24.54 vs 37.9, P < 0.05); Table 4 also marks the baseline schizotypal difference but not the larger baseline perceptual-symptom difference (13.43 (9.20) vs 1.12 (1.56); editors' calculation, Welch t ≈ 5.5), although the Method says post hoc tests were run only after significant interactions (p. 1453).
reporting_issues.consequence: The significance markers in Table 4 cannot be relied on; baseline mood and subjective-symptom differences should not be cited from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Identical values appear in unrelated cells: the ketamine group's baseline serial sevens score (24.8 (8.16), p. 1456) equals the controls' baseline schizotypal total (24.8 (8.16), Table 4, p. 1455); the controls' baseline discontentedness and calm scores are 37.92 (9.59) and 37.9 (9.59); and both groups' baseline cognitive-symptom SDs are 20.08 (Table 4). Table 4 also leaves a parenthesis unclosed (12.12 (12.61).
reporting_issues.consequence: Suggests transcription errors in the tables; these cells should not be cited without the authors' data.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that one of the ketamine participants from the sample of 18 had developed schizophrenia (p. 1459), but the Method states that this person was excluded, leaving 18 from the original ketamine group (p. 1452).
reporting_issues.consequence: The person was not in the analysed sample; no statement about schizophrenia among people who use ketamine can rest on this study beyond the existence of one excluded case.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper says the same battery was used at both sessions, but describes the speed of comprehension test as 200 sentences and the delayed prose recall as following a delay of about 20 minutes (p. 1453), whereas both baseline studies describe 100 sentences and a delay of 15 minutes or about 15 minutes (Curran & Morgan, 2000, p. 578; Curran & Monaghan, 2001, p. 752).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the description is wrong or the follow-up tasks differed from the baseline ones; a changed task would confound the time and group × time effects on these two measures.

reporting_issues.issue: The follow-up depression difference is printed as U = 55.5, P < 0.031 (p. 1454; Table 1 marks P < 0.05), but U = 55.5 for groups of 18 and 10 gives a two-tailed p of about 0.10 (one-tailed about 0.05; normal approximation and exact null distribution, editors' calculation); a t-test on the printed means and SDs gives about 0.04 (Welch about 0.02). The trend printed for years of cannabis use (U = 46.5, P = 0.052) gives about 0.04 with the same group sizes, while the three subjective-effects tests on p. 1456 (U = 34, 21 and 39.5) reproduce their printed P values.
reporting_issues.consequence: The follow-up depression difference is less secure than printed and should be cited with the recalculation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that the participants of Curran & Morgan (2000) did not differ from controls on depression at baseline (p. 1459), but that paper reports higher HADS depression scores in its ketamine group on both test days, including the drug-free session 3 days after use that this paper uses as baseline (4.30 against 1.68; group F(1,32) = 19.4, p<0.001; Curran & Morgan, 2000, pp. 581, 585).
reporting_issues.consequence: The follow-up depression difference cannot be read as new since the first testing: for the participants of the 2000 study a difference was already present at baseline.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper cites Morgan et al. (2004a), which its reference list gives as the team's Neuropsychopharmacology laboratory study (29, 208–218), for the finding that healthy volunteers showed no residual effects 3 days after a single dose (pp. 1451, 1457), and in the same paragraph on p. 1451 for volunteers liking ketamine and wanting more of it, which is the subject of the Psychopharmacology paper listed as 2004b (172, 298–308); Morgan et al. (2009, p. 78) cites the Psychopharmacology paper for the 3-day finding.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which laboratory study showed no residual effect 3 days after a dose cannot be established from the team's papers; the finding should be cited only as the team's second-hand statement.
